title: How Supercontinents Come and Go
objective: After this level you can explain the supercontinent cycle, in which continents gather, split apart and gather again.
summary: Continents gather into supercontinents, split as oceans open, and return as old ocean floor sinks, every 300 to 500 million years. Columbia and Rodinia came before Pangaea.

cards.headline: Pangaea wasn't the first supercontinent, and it won't be the last.
cards.body: You met Pangaea in World Geography. It turns out the continents have gathered and scattered again and again, like dancers who keep finding each other on a very slow dance floor.

cards.headline: A cycle, not a one-off
cards.body: A supercontinent holds the vast majority of Earth's land in one mass. Geologists now see them as part of a cycle: continents gather, split apart and gather again, roughly every 300 to 500 million years. The engine is slow churning, or convection, in Earth's mantle.

cards.headline: How oceans open and close
cards.body: When a supercontinent breaks up, new oceans open between the pieces. But ocean floor doesn't last forever. Oceanic plates eventually sink back into the mantle, a process called subduction, and as an ocean closes, the continents on either side are drawn back together. Then the whole cycle starts again.
cards.callout: Gather, split, open an ocean, sink it, gather again

options.rationale: Siccar Point is a Scottish cliff.

questions.explanation: Rodinia existed from about 1.2 billion to 750 million years ago, long before Pangaea.

questions.prompt: How does an ocean between two continents eventually close?

options.label: Its water slowly evaporates away
options.rationale: The ocean floor itself disappears, not just the water.

options.label: Its ocean floor sinks back into the mantle by subduction
Rivers fill it with sediment
options.rationale: Sediment can't close an ocean basin.

options.label: The continents shrink until the gap disappears
options.rationale: Continents move; they don't shrink away.

questions.explanation: Oceanic plates sink back into the mantle, and as the ocean closes the continents are drawn together.

questions.prompt: Pangaea assembled about 299 to 273 million years ago. Which era of the geologic time scale was that?

options.label: The Mesozoic
options.rationale: The Mesozoic began about 252 million years ago.

options.label: The Cenozoic
options.rationale: The Cenozoic began about 66 million years ago.

options.label: The Hadean
options.rationale: The Hadean is an eon at the very start of Earth's history.

questions.explanation: Anything older than about 252 million years but inside the Phanerozoic falls in the Paleozoic Era.
